title: Every Red Delicious is one tree
teaches: Why an apple seed almost never grows the apple it came from, how grafting copies a tree by joining cambium to cambium, how rootstocks set a tree's size, and the apples of Washington

blocks.text: Eat a good apple, plant its seeds, and wait the five to ten years it takes the trees to fruit. Almost every tree gives a different apple, and most of them are small, hard and sour, fit only for cider or for pigs. The pioneer nurseryman John Chapman, Johnny Appleseed, planted apple seeds across Ohio and Indiana in the early 1800s, and the orchards that grew from them were mostly for hard cider. Apples don't come true from seed.

Yet every Red Delicious apple ever sold grew on a tree that is a copy of one tree. In the early 1870s a seedling came up out of line in Jesse Hiatt's orchard near Peru, Iowa. Hiatt cut it down; it grew back, and he let it grow. Its fruit was striped red and sweet. In 1893 he sent it to a fruit contest held by the Stark Brothers nursery of Missouri, which bought the rights and renamed it Delicious. Every Red Delicious tree since has been grown from shoots cut from that tree, or from its copies, and grafted.

Lesson C1 showed that each parent passes on one of its two copies of each gene, at random. A true-breeding pea has two identical copies of nearly every gene, so its offspring are like it. An apple tree is the opposite. Nearly all apple varieties can't fertilise themselves or any flower of the same variety, so almost every apple seed is a cross, with pollen from some other tree, and generations of such crosses have left apples with two different copies of a great many genes. Each seed gets a new random mix. A great apple is a rare lucky combination, and its seeds break the combination up.

blocks.caption: A hundred trees grown from one good apple's seeds, and a hundred grafted. A model.

blocks.text: So apples are copied, not grown from seed. A **graft** joins a short length of shoot from the tree to be copied, the **scion**, onto the roots and lower stem of another young tree, the **rootstock**. People have done this for well over two thousand years. What makes it work is the cambium, lesson 16's thin layer under the bark that makes new wood on its inside and new phloem on its outside. It is the only layer of a woody stem whose cells are still dividing.

blocks.caption: A scion set on a rootstock's cut end, seen from above.
blocks.task: Guess, then line the cambium up

blocks.text: The grafter cuts both pieces so their cambium meets along at least one edge, and binds them tight. Within weeks the cambium cells on each side grow into the gap, mingle, and make new xylem and phloem that join the two. From then on the scion's leaves feed the roots and the roots water the scion, and the branches that grow from the scion carry its genes, and its apples, faithfully, apart from the rare mutation described below. A tree in your garden labelled Gala is a Gala scion on someone else's roots.

The rootstock does more than hold the tree up. From 1912 the East Malling research station in Kent, England, collected and tested apple rootstocks, and found that some keep any scion grafted onto them small. On the rootstock called M9 an apple tree stays two or three metres tall and bears fruit in its second or third year, where the same variety on its own roots would grow into a big tree taking eight years to fruit. Modern orchards are rows of such small trees on wires, picked from the ground or short ladders.

Copies can still change. Now and then a single bud mutates and grows into a branch whose fruit is different, a **sport**. Growers looking for redder Red Delicious grafted the reddest sports for decades, and ended up with a deep red apple that looked perfect and, many buyers felt, had lost much of its taste.

Washington grows most of the fresh apples sold in the United States, in irrigated valleys east of the Cascades around Wenatchee, Yakima and the Okanogan, where dry sunny summers mean few fungal diseases and cold nights colour the fruit. For most of the twentieth century its main apple was Red Delicious. It has since given way to newer varieties, including Cosmic Crisp, bred at Washington State University from a 1997 cross of Enterprise and Honeycrisp: one of thousands of seedlings tested, and the rare good one, now grafted onto millions of trees.

The wild ancestor of the apple, *Malus sieversii*, still grows in the forests of the Tian Shan mountains in Kazakhstan, where, like trees grown from seed in any orchard, each tree's apples are different. Look at an apple tree in winter for the graft union, a bulge in the trunk just above the ground where scion meets rootstock.

blocks.caption: Five questions on apples and grafting
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Why do trees grown from a good apple's seeds give mostly poor apples?
choices: Each seed is a new random mix of two parents' many different gene copies
The seeds come from the weakest flowers
Seedling trees fruit too young to ripen well
items.why: Apples can't self-fertilise and carry two different copies of many genes, so each seed is a new combination.

items.ask: In a graft, which layers must meet?
choices: The cambium of scion and rootstock
items.why: The cambium is the only layer still dividing. Its cells grow across the join and connect xylem and phloem.

items.ask: What sets how tall a grafted apple tree grows?
choices: How deeply the graft is buried
items.why: Dwarfing rootstocks such as M9 keep any variety grafted onto them small.

items.ask: Why does a Gala scion grafted onto another variety's roots bear Gala apples?
choices: The branches grow from the Gala scion and carry its genes
The rootstock is also a Gala
The rootstock's genes are switched off by the graft
items.why: Everything above the graft grows from the scion, a piece of the original Gala tree.

choices: A branch grown from a mutated bud, with different fruit
A rootstock grown from a cutting
A rootstock that keeps trees small
items.why: Sports appear on a single tree, and can be grafted to make a new strain, like the redder Red Delicious.

summary: **Apples don't come true from seed.** Most seedlings give small, sour fruit.
**Each seed is a new mix.** Apples can't self-fertilise and carry two different copies of many genes (lesson C1).
**Every Red Delicious descends by grafting from one tree.** A chance seedling in Jesse Hiatt's Iowa orchard in the 1870s.
**Grafting joins cambium to cambium.** The only dividing layer (lesson 16) grows across the cut and joins xylem and phloem.
**The rootstock sets the size.** On M9 an apple stays small and fruits in two or three years.
**A sport is a mutated bud.** Grafting the reddest sports made Red Delicious redder and, many said, less tasty.
